cita: Xie et al. (2026). MEMO: Memory-Augmented Model Context Optimization for Robust Multi-Turn Multi-Agent LLM Games.
problema: Multi-turn, multi-agent LLM game evaluations exhibit substantial run-to-run variance because small early deviations compound across turns and are amplified by multi-agent coupling, biasing win-rate estimates and destabilizing model rankings across repeated tournaments; static or single-batch prompt optimization cannot adapt to rare, decisive states that recur across game rounds.
mecanismo: MEMO couples tournament-based context evolution (TrueSkill Bayesian skill rating with a conservative lower-confidence-bound score to select/discard candidate contexts across self-play generations) with a persistent memory bank Bmem that distills structured typed insights from sampled trajectory reflections and reconciles them via CRUD-style Add/Remove/Edit merge operations (conflicting insights mutually removed, similar ones merged/generalized); a prioritized replay buffer resamples rare/decisive game-state prefixes (inverse-frequency priority) to improve coverage, and the highest-scoring evolved context is reinjected as inference-time priors for future rounds.
evaluacion: Five text-based games from TextArena/SPIN-Bench (negotiation, imperfect-information, perfect-information categories) with GPT-4o-mini and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct backbones, compared against static prompting (baseline, CoT, ToT), prompt optimization (TextGrad, MIPRO, GEPA) and RL self-play (UnstableBaselines, SPIRAL) baselines using mean win rate and relative standard error (RSE) across 3 optimization runs plus a module ablation (Tournament/Memory/Replay) and cross-task transfer analysis.
numeros_clave: MEMO raises mean win rate from 25.1% to 49.5% (GPT-4o-mini) and 20.9% to 44.3% (Qwen-2.5-7B) using 2,000 self-play games (19x fewer than RL's 38,000); lowest RSE 6.4% vs MIPRO's 12.4%; ablation Table 3: mean win rate 23.8% (prompt-opt alone) -> 34.2% (+Memory, +10.4) -> 48.1% (Tournament+Memory, +24.3) -> 50.2% (+Replay, +26.4); output-token cost 91K vs MIPRO 354K / GEPA 113K (Table 1).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Ablation Table 3 isolates that Memory alone contributes the largest single jump (+10.4pp) and Tournament+Memory jointly (+24.3pp) dominates Tournament-only (+3.3pp) or Replay-only gains -- a direct measured confirmation that MF's CONSOLIDACION (retained, merged insights) is the dominant lever, not exploration alone.

The memory bank's Add/Remove/Edit merge rule (SS3.2) explicitly detects and deletes CONTRADICTORY insights (both sides removed) rather than storing conflicting facts side-by-side, a concrete single-source-of-truth reconciliation policy relevant to MF's COSTURAS anchor.

Table 1 shows MEMO uses ~91K output tokens vs 354K (MIPRO) and 113K (GEPA) while matching/beating their win rates, and needs 19x fewer self-play games than RL -- a strong confirmation of MF's context/sample-economy thesis.

notes: Table 2 (main win-rate/RSE results) and Table 3 (module ablation) anchor the numbers; Fig.1 visualizes the stability-vs-win-rate and sample-efficiency comparisons; Table 4 tests cross-game generalization of learned context.

cita: Wang et al. (2026). VeriAgent: A Tool-Integrated Multi-Agent System with Evolving Memory for PPA-Aware RTL Code Generation.
problema: LLM-based RTL (Verilog) code generation focuses mostly on functional correctness while overlooking Power/Performance/Area (PPA) physical-design metrics, and existing systems use EDA-toolchain feedback only shallowly (single-round), lacking any long-term optimization memory to accumulate and refine knowledge across design iterations.
mecanismo: VeriAgent runs a closed-loop multi-agent workflow (Programmer, Correctness, PPA agents + EDA tools) where a Memory Manager extracts structured memory nodes (trigger condition, natural-language guidance, metadata) from execution trajectories into three types -- Rule Memory (general design constraints), Structure Memory (code-pattern-to-optimization mappings), EDA Signal Memory (PPA-signal-to-optimization mappings); before each generation step an LLM semantically matches context against stored triggers to activate top-K relevant nodes injected into agent prompts, and after each task an LLM-based Decide module inserts/refines/discards each candidate memory node against the top-K most-similar existing nodes (Algorithm 1).
evaluacion: VerilogEval (Machine/Human tracks, pass@1/5/10) and RTLLM v1.1 (functional) / v2.0 (PPA, via Yosys+OpenROAD NanGate45 synthesis) benchmarks with GPT-4o and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview backbones, compared against training-based SOTA (CraftRTL, ChipSeek-R1, etc.) and training-free direct prompting, plus an ablation removing Memory / Tool Feedback / PPA Analyzer and pairwise PPA win-rate vs VeriPPA/ChipSeek-R1.
numeros_clave: VeriAgent(Gemini-3-pro) reaches 97.9% pass@1 VerilogEval-Machine / 98.1% Human / 100% RTLLM Syn@5; RTLLM v2.0 relative PPA score 8.539 (Gemini-3) / 5.119 (GPT-4o) vs original=1.0, ChipSeek-R1=2.196; ablation Table 3: removing Memory drops PPA score from 5.119 to 3.839 (GPT-4o) and 8.539 to 6.541 (Gemini-3).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Ablation Table 3 shows removing the memory mechanism alone drops the PPA score from 5.119 to 3.839 (GPT-4o) and 8.539 to 6.541 (Gemini-3) -- a clean, isolated measurement confirming that consolidating optimization experience into reusable memory nodes materially improves outcomes, supporting MF's CONSOLIDACION thesis.

Memory nodes are explicit (trigger, guidance, metadata) typed structures activated via LLM semantic matching against triggers (SS2.3.2), not raw log retrieval -- a derived, typed index layer over raw EDA tool output relevant to MF's TIER-INDICE/TIER-DOCS framing.

Three parallel memory types (Rule/Structure/EDA Signal) are each triggered and retrieved through one shared Memory Manager interface (Fig.1), illustrating a multi-typed-but-single-manager seam relevant to MF's COSTURAS question, without discussing cross-type conflict resolution explicitly.

notes: Table 1 (functional correctness) and Table 2 (PPA scores per design) anchor the primary numbers; Table 3 (component ablation) isolates the memory contribution; Fig.1 diagrams the closed-loop multi-agent + Memory Manager architecture (SS2).

cita: Rana et al. (2026). Oblivion: Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation.
problema: Memory-augmented LLM agents rely on 'always-on' retrieval and 'flat' undifferentiated memory storage, causing high interference (needle-in-a-haystack degradation as stores grow) and unnecessary latency/cost, and typically resort to hard deletion rather than graceful, reversible forgetting to manage context limits.
mecanismo: Oblivion decouples memory control into a read path and a write path over a hierarchical memory (L1 Dynamic Procedural cluster index, L2 timestamped Semantic facts, L3 Preemptive Episodic entries): the Decayer gates retrieval by an uncertainty score (LLM-judge + embedding similarity) and computes an Ebbinghaus-inspired exponential retention score Rt(c)=exp(-nt(c)/St(c)) per cluster (utility+frequency-modulated stability, decay temperature T) so unused clusters fade in accessibility (never deleted) while frequently-used ones decay slowly; when triggered, the Activator decomposes the query into a DAG of sub-queries for targeted L2/L3 retrieval; on the write path a Recognizer performs credit assignment (which memories actually contributed to the response) and a Memory Manager reinforces only those clusters' utility, implementing decay-driven (not deletion-driven) forgetting.
evaluacion: LongMemEval (500 human-curated multi-session QA questions, Oracle vs. noisy-S settings) and GoodAI-LTM (33 dynamic long-horizon interaction tests, Isolated/2K/32K/120K memory-span settings) across 4 backbones (Phi-4-mini, Qwen3-30B-A3B, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini) vs. direct (LME-RFT/FullCtx) and memory (EverMemOS/BeyondPrompts) baselines, plus a memory-hierarchy ablation (L1/L2/L3 combinations) and a computational-efficiency (token/latency/cost) analysis.
numeros_clave: LongMemEval-S GPT-4.1-mini: Oblivion 90.60% avg accuracy vs LME-RFT-direct 89.00% and EverMemOS-memory 81.27%; GoodAI-LTM GPT-4.1-mini 120K: Oblivion 6.70 solved scenarios vs FullCtx 6.42; token cost reduced 73% (120K) and 67% (32K) vs FullCtx (Table 4); hierarchy ablation Table 3: full L1+L2+L3 stack (M5) reaches 90.60% (LongMemEval-S) / 8.41 (GoodAI-LTM 2K) vs single-layer 86.40%/6.14.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Oblivion reframes forgetting as decay-driven REDUCED ACCESSIBILITY rather than deletion (SS2.2-2.3: memories 'never deleted from D, preserving reactivatability') -- directly relevant to MF's NEGATIVO anchor if MF also treats non-recall as a graded signal rather than binary erase, though Oblivion's target is efficiency/interference, not explicit negative-knowledge capture.

Table 4 measures 73%/67% token-cost reduction at 120K/32K memory spans via uncertainty-gated (not always-on) retrieval while improving/matching accuracy -- a strong quantitative confirmation of MF's context-economy thesis that gating retrieval by need beats always-on recall.

L2 Semantic Memory stores timestamped facts specifically to resolve 'world drift' (temporal inconsistency, prioritizing currently-valid facts over outdated ones, SS2.1) -- a concrete staleness-resolution mechanism directly relevant to MF's FIDELIDAD anchor.

notes: Table 1 (LongMemEval) and Table 2 (GoodAI-LTM) anchor main results; Table 3 isolates the L1/L2/L3 hierarchy contribution; Table 4 anchors the token/latency/cost tradeoff; Fig.2 visualizes the Ebbinghaus decay/reinforcement curves (SS5.1).

cita: Wu et al. (2026). LongMemEval-V2: Evaluating Long-Term Agent Memory Toward Experienced Colleagues.
problema: Existing agent-memory benchmarks mostly evaluate personalized user-chat histories, short traces, or indirect downstream task success, leaving open whether memory systems can directly internalize environment-specific experience (interface affordances, state dynamics, workflows, recurring failure modes/gotchas) the way an 'experienced colleague' would across a genuinely long (25M-115M token) multi-trajectory haystack.
mecanismo: LME-V2 formalizes memory as a context-gathering task with Insert(trajectory)/Query(question) APIs over a haystack of up to 500 trajectories; the paper's own baseline AgentRunbook-R maintains three separate LLM-controller-queried knowledge pools (raw state-observation slices, state-transition events, high-level strategy/gotcha notes) retrieved via multi-stream dense queries, while AgentRunbook-C instead stores raw trajectories as files and invokes an augmented coding-agent (with workflow docs, memory manifests, helper inspection scripts) to search/inspect/assemble evidence at query time, trading latency for accuracy.
evaluacion: 451 manually curated questions (five memory abilities: static state recall, dynamic state tracking, workflow knowledge, environment gotchas, premise awareness) over web-agent trajectories from WebArena/WorkArena, in Small (100-trajectory/25M-token) and Medium (500-trajectory/115M-token) haystack tiers, comparing a simple RAG baseline, AgentRunbook-R, an off-the-shelf Codex coding-agent baseline, and AgentRunbook-C, measured by answer accuracy and query latency; pilot studies test frontier-LLM parametric-knowledge-only performance and oracle-trajectory upper bounds.
numeros_clave: Simple RAG: 40.1% overall accuracy; AgentRunbook-R: 57.8%; off-the-shelf Codex coding agent: 69.3% accuracy but ~182s/query (6.9x slower than AgentRunbook-R); AgentRunbook-C: best overall 72.5% accuracy while 32% faster than Codex; frontier LLMs with no trajectory context reach only up to 14.1% best-model accuracy (Fig.4), confirming questions are not answerable from parametric knowledge alone.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: AgentRunbook-R's separate 'procedure and hint note pool' explicitly consolidates trajectory-level notes into reusable typed workflow/gotcha knowledge (SS4.1), and the pilot study shows raw long-context prompting or slices alone underperform structured notes (Fig.4: 59.6% oracle-trajectories vs 82.5% oracle-slices+notes) -- confirms MF's TIER-DOCS thesis that typed narrative beats raw log dumping.

AgentRunbook-C achieves the best accuracy (72.5%) while being 32% faster than the raw coding-agent baseline (69.3% at 182s/query) purely from added scaffolding (workflow doc, manifests, helper scripts) -- directly supports MF's context/latency-economy thesis that structuring the retrieval interface (not just having more compute) is the lever.

The benchmark's central finding -- that a naive RAG baseline (40.1%) is dramatically outperformed by structured multi-pool retrieval (57.8%) and coding-agent-based evidence assembly (72.5%) -- is a MEASURED demonstration that retrieval design/mechanism, not mere embedding similarity, determines memory quality, aligning with MF's G-M2 stance.

notes: SS5 main results (RAG 40.1% / AgentRunbook-R 57.8% / Codex 69.3% / AgentRunbook-C 72.5%) and Fig.4 pilot studies anchor the numbers; Table 1 situates LME-V2's scale (25M-115M tokens) against prior benchmarks; Fig.5 diagrams both AgentRunbook variants (SS4).

cita: Choi et al. (2026). PREPING: Building Agent Memory without Tasks.
problema: Agent memory construction methods (offline from curated demonstrations, or online from post-deployment interactions) both require target-environment task experience that is unavailable for a newly connected environment, leaving a 'cold-start gap': the agent has no procedural memory when it first needs it, exposing users to early failures during online construction.
mecanismo: PREPING separates a construction-time Proposer memory (tracks prior synthetic-practice history, tool/workflow coverage imbalance, and grounded-environment facts observed during execution) from deployment-facing Solver memory: a Proposer generates synthetic tasks conditioned on Proposer memory (coverage-seeking, environment-grounded, avoiding redundancy), a Solver executes them producing trajectories, and a Validator scores feasibility+completion; only Validator-approved (feasibility=5) task-trajectory pairs are distilled (reflector-curator style, ACE-inspired) into Solver memory, while ALL outcomes (including rejected/infeasible ones) update Proposer memory to steer future proposals away from repeated failure modes -- an asymmetric write-gate separating what shapes practice from what becomes deployed procedural guidance.
evaluacion: AppWorld (stateful app tasks, Test-Normal/Test-Challenge splits), BFCL v3 (function calling: Base/Long-Context/Missing-Parameter/Missing-Function), and MCP-Universe (Repository/Financial/3D/Browser categories); compared against pre-task baselines (Base no-memory, Direct-Memory-from-docs, Random/Guided free-form Exploration) and task-informed reference methods (ACE-Offline, ACE-Online), plus a component ablation (Validator gating / environment info / practice history) and a warm-start experiment (PREPING+ACE).
numeros_clave: PREPING improves average score over Base by 17.1pp (AppWorld), 19.3pp (BFCL v3), 5.4pp (MCP-Universe) with zero target-task experience, exceeding ACE-Offline on AppWorld (72.2 vs 69.0 avg) and near/surpassing ACE-Online on BFCL v3; PREPING+ACE warm-start improves AppWorld from 71.3 to 76.3 avg; deployment cost 2.99x lower on AppWorld and 2.23x lower on BFCL v3 than ACE-Online when frozen; ablation Table 2: disabling Validator+Env-Info+Practice-History drops AppWorld score from 83.7/70.2 to 47.8/26.8.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The Validator's feasibility=5 threshold is an explicit, outcome-gated write trigger deciding what enters Solver memory (SS3.4), while a SEPARATE asymmetric channel (Proposer memory) absorbs ALL outcomes including rejects to steer future practice -- a two-tier write-discipline MF's G-M1 (discretionary write) could adopt: gate the durable store, but still learn from rejects elsewhere.

Proposer memory explicitly records failure/infeasibility reasons for REJECTED tasks (not just successes) to prevent future proposals from repeating the same failure modes (SS3.3) -- a concrete negative-knowledge mechanism (what NOT to try again) relevant to MF's NEGATIVO anchor, even though F does not flag NEGATIVO for this paper.

Frozen pre-task memory reduces deployment-time cost by 2.99x (AppWorld) and 2.23x (BFCL v3) vs. online memory construction (ACE-Online) by avoiding per-task memory-update calls -- a direct confirmation of MF's context/cost-economy thesis for WHEN to write vs. defer.

notes: Table 1 (main pre-task vs task-informed results) and Table 2 (component ablation) anchor the numbers; Table 3 and Fig.3 show the PREPING+ACE warm-start cold-start mitigation; Fig.1 (right) visualizes tool-coverage-vs-tested-tasks curves.

cita: Jin et al. (2026). SE-GA: Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution for GUI Agents.
problema: GUI agents on multi-step tasks are limited by constrained context windows (losing early critical information, causing error accumulation across long horizons) and by static policies trained on fixed datasets that cannot reuse past successful strategies or adapt to dynamic layout/environment changes.
mecanismo: SE-GA's Test-Time Memory Extension (TTME) maintains a hierarchical memory M=(M_EPI, M_SEM, M_EXP): episodic memory is a sliding-window (horizon H) buffer of recent action transitions; semantic memory stores abstract interaction rules retrieved by cosine similarity of instruction embeddings; experiential memory stores raw trajectories plus reflective summaries retrieved via a hybrid intent+visual-similarity score, all three contexts concatenated into the agent's input at each decision step. Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution (MASE) then trains on this TTME-collected data in two stages: Grounding SFT (behavior cloning on memory-augmented context) followed by GRPO-based Self-Evolution Training with token-level importance ratios, adaptive clipping, a hierarchical format+accuracy reward, and a Hindsight Goal-Shifting mechanism that relabels prefix subsequences of FAILED trajectories as successes for whatever alternative sub-goal they actually achieved, converting failures into usable supervision.
evaluacion: ScreenSpot (grounding), AndroidControl-Low/High and GUIOdyssey (step-wise type/grounding/success-rate), and AndroidWorld (online dynamic generalization), using Qwen2.5-VL-7B as backbone, compared against 15 baselines (closed-source VLMs, generalist open-source VLMs, specialized GUI agents like UI-TARS/OS-Atlas/Aguvis), plus implicit ablation of TTME components and the Hindsight Goal-Shifting mechanism.
numeros_clave: 89.0% avg success on ScreenSpot (vs UI-TARS-72B 88.4%, OS-Atlas 82.5%); 75.8% success rate on AndroidControl-High (abstract); AndroidControl-Low: SR 88.6% (vs UI-TARS 91.3%), grounding 92.5% (best in Table 2); significant AndroidWorld generalization gains reported (abstract, dynamic online benchmark).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: plan_estado=SI per extraction; TTME's episodic memory (M_EPI) is a sliding-window transition history tracking CURRENT task progress (SS4.1.1), functioning as an implicit plan/state tracker rather than an explicit persisted plan-state artifact distinct from raw interaction history.

MASE's Hindsight Goal-Shifting mechanism (SS4.2.2) relabels FAILED trajectory prefixes as successes for whichever sub-goal they actually achieved, converting otherwise-discarded experience into reusable training/memory signal -- a concrete failure-to-recipe promotion pattern relevant to MF's CONSOLIDACION anchor.

Three memory types (episodic/semantic/experiential) are retrieved by three DIFFERENT similarity mechanisms (recency window, text-embedding cosine, hybrid intent+visual) and simply concatenated into one prompt (SS4.1), illustrating a multi-store/multi-key design relevant to MF's COSTURAS question without an explicit single-key reconciliation policy.

notes: Table 1 (ScreenSpot) and Table 2 (AndroidControl/GUIOdyssey) anchor the numbers; abstract reports AndroidWorld and AndroidControl-High headline figures not fully tabulated in the read excerpt; SS4.2 formalizes MASE's two-stage GRPO training with Hindsight Goal-Shifting (Eq.17).
